common_name: Mary Stoker Chrysanthemum (Apricot-Yellow Heritage Rubellum Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; raised by Amos Perry in England and long grown as one of the classic hardy rubellum mums.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mary Stoker is a Chrysanthemum x rubellum selection carrying an RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized for its unusual soft apricot-yellow single daisy flowers with a darker gold-green center, a warmer, muddier tone than the typical pink or bronze rubellum mums. It blooms from late September into October, ahead of many hardy mums, giving reliable color before the first hard frosts. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to encourage bushy, self-supporting growth, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Mary Stoker' Plant Profile
North Carolina State University Extension — Hardy Chrysanthemums for Southern Gardens

common_name: Nancy Perry Chrysanthemum (Rose-Pink Heritage Rubellum Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; like other rubellum-type mums, Nancy Perry is a long-lived garden perennial rather than a disposable florist pot mum.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Nancy Perry is a Chrysanthemum x rubellum selection bred by the Perry nursery family in England, closely related to Clara Curtis and Sheffield Pink but with a deeper, more saturated rose-pink single daisy flower and a neat, clump-forming habit. It blooms heavily from late summer into fall, providing strong late-season color while remaining more compact and self-supporting than the taller rubellum cultivars. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to keep growth dense, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to prevent crowding.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Nancy Perry' Plant Profile
North Carolina State University Extension — Hardy Chrysanthemums for Southern Gardens

common_name: Innocence Chrysanthemum (Pale Pink Heritage Rubellum Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Innocence is another Amos Perry-raised rubellum selection from the same English breeding line as Clara Curtis, Sheffield Pink, and Mary Stoker.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Innocence bears single daisy flowers that open a soft shell-pink with a golden-yellow center, paler and gentler in tone than its rubellum relatives Clara Curtis and Sheffield Pink. It blooms from early to mid fall, forming loose, spreading colonies over time in the manner typical of rubellum-type hardy mums. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to promote compact, floriferous growth, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Innocence' Plant Profile
North Carolina State University Extension — Hardy Chrysanthemums for Southern Gardens

common_name: Single Apricot Korean Chrysanthemum (Hardy Single-Flowered Korean-Type Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish well before the fall bloom flush; Korean-type mums descend from open-pollinated crosses between Chrysanthemum indicum and C. morifolium and are valued for exceptional garden hardiness.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Single Apricot Korean produces abundant single daisy flowers in warm apricot-orange with a golden-yellow center, held on sturdy, well-branched stems typical of the old-fashioned Korean mum strain. It blooms reliably from late summer into fall and, unlike many modern florist mums, survives winters in the open garden without lifting where hardy. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build a dense, self-supporting mound, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain bloom quality.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Hardy Chrysanthemums for Southern Gardens
